Empirical Research Plan  
“Colonial Land-Tenure Systems and Contemporary Economic Performance in India”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Geographic Regression-Discontinuity Design (GRDD, a border discontinuity design).

Rationale  
• Treatment (type of colonial tenure) varies sharply at historical administrative borders that were drawn by the British largely for logistical convenience, not local economic fundamentals.  
• Modern district boundaries still map closely to those colonial boundaries, allowing us to treat the border as an exogenous cutoff in geographic space.  
• Because treatment is time-invariant (institutions fixed c. 1830-1947) and outcomes are observed post-1960, time-series designs (DID or event study) are less informative, while IVs are hard to justify without new instruments.  
• GRDD lets us compare districts (or sub-district polygons within a small buffer) that are spatially adjacent but have different colonial regimes, holding constant geography, climate, culture, and market access up to smooth functions of distance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 if a location lay inside a district that was under Zamindari (landlord-based) revenue settlement during British rule; 0 otherwise (Ryotwari or Mahalwari, both non-landlord).

Control group  
Adjacent locations just across the historical border that were governed by Ryotwari/Mahalwari settlements.

Running variable & cutoff  
Running variable r_i = signed minimum distance (in km) of location i to the closest historical tenure boundary.  
Cutoff r_i = 0 (exact boundary). r_i < 0 ⇒ treated, r_i > 0 ⇒ control.

Treatment timing  
One-shot assignment in the 19th century; outcomes measured 1960–present. No staggered timing needed for GRDD.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the boundary.  
Economic outcomes would evolve smoothly in the absence of the tenure regime; any sharp discontinuity comes from treatment.

Plausibility: British administrators chose tenure types based on administrative convenience and historical precedent, not sharp changes in soil or pre-colonial prosperity. We will inspect pre-colonial covariates (e.g., 1901 population density, elevation, rainfall) for balance.

A2. No sorting or manipulation around the cutoff.  
District borders were fixed long before modern outcomes and migration is limited relative to district area; economic agents cannot “choose” sides retroactively.

A3. No other policies jump exactly at the same boundary.  
Because district-level policies (e.g., post-independence land reforms, public spending) are determined by state or national governments, they do not discontinuously change at the historical settlement line once geography is controlled for.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Geographic or agro-climatic discontinuities coincide with settlement borders.  
• Mitigation: control flexibly for elevation, rainfall, soil quality; run placebo RD on these observables; use extremely narrow bandwidths (e.g., ≤50 km).  

T2. Post-independence administrative redistricting blurs historical borders.  
• Mitigation: digitise original colonial maps; assign treatment at the sub-district polygon level; restrict analysis to buffer zones where historical and current borders overlap; robustness check dropping districts created after 1971.

T3. Spatial spillovers (e.g., technology diffusion) across the boundary attenuate effects.  
• Mitigation: include border-pair fixed effects (compare each treated polygon only with its matched neighbour); cluster SEs by border segment; interpret estimates as local average treatment effect net of spillovers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Required packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(sf)             # spatial operations
library(fixest)         # fast fixed-effects regressions
library(rdrobust)       # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Economic outcomes at district level
econ <- fread("india_district_outcomes.csv")            # columns: dist_id, year, ag_prod, infra, literacy, controls...
# Shapefile of current districts
dist_shp <- st_read("india_district_shapefile.shp")     # contains dist_id
# Raster or shapefile of historical settlement boundaries
settle_bound <- st_read("colonial_tenure_boundary.shp") # polygons with var 'tenure'

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge and construct treatment
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Spatial join: assign each modern district the colonial tenure that covered
# the largest share of its area
dist_tenure <- st_join(dist_shp, settle_bound, join = st_intersects) |>
  group_by(dist_id) |>
  summarise(zam_share = mean(tenure == "Zamindari", na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(zamindari = as.integer(zam_share > 0.5)) |>  # majority rule
  st_drop_geometry()

# Merge with outcomes
econ <- merge(econ, dist_tenure, by = "dist_id")

# Generate controls
econ[, ln_pop1961 := log(pop1961)]
econ[, rain_mean := scale(rainfall_mm)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main RD specification (local linear, border FE)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Create buffer (e.g., ±100 km) around boundary
buffer <- 100000  # meters
border_strip <- st_buffer(settle_bound, dist = buffer)

# Intersect districts with strip, keep only overlap
strip_data <- st_intersection(dist_shp, border_strip) |>
  st_centroid()                                        # use centroid as location

# Compute signed distance to boundary
strip_data$dist2bound <- st_distance(strip_data, settle_bound)
# Make signed: negative if in Zamindari area
strip_data$dist2bound <- ifelse(strip_data$zamindari==1,
                                -as.numeric(strip_data$dist2bound),
                                 as.numeric(strip_data$dist2bound))

# Merge outcomes for, say, 2011 census wave
strip_econ <- merge(strip_data |> st_drop_geometry(),
                    econ[year==2011],
                    by="dist_id")

# Local linear RD with rdrobust
rd <- rdrobust(y = strip_econ$ag_prod, x = strip_econ$dist2bound,
               covs = strip_econ[,.(ln_pop1961,rain_mean,elevation)],
               kernel = "triangular")
summary(rd)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Border-pair fixed-effects OLS (within a 50 km bandwidth)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
bw <- 50000
ols_data <- strip_econ[abs(dist2bound) <= bw]

# Create matched border pair FE: concatenate IDs of closest cross-border neighbours
# (simplified example)
ols_data[, pair_id := as.factor(nearest_border_id)]

est <- feols(ag_prod ~ zamindari + ln_pop1961 + rain_mean | pair_id,
             data = ols_data, cluster = ~pair_id)
summary(est)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: different bandwidth + placebo outcome (1901 pop density)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
for(bw in c(30000,70000,100000)){
  cat("\nBandwidth:", bw/1000,"km\n")
  dat <- strip_econ[abs(dist2bound) <= bw]
  print(feols(ag_prod ~ zamindari + ln_pop1961 + rain_mean | pair_id,
              data = dat, cluster = ~pair_id))
}

# Placebo on pre-treatment outcome
feols(pop_density1901 ~ zamindari | pair_id,
      data = ols_data, cluster = ~pair_id)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Based on the literature (e.g., Banerjee & Iyer 2005), landlord (Zamindari) areas are likely to exhibit:  
• Lower agricultural productivity (≈ 5–10 percentage-points less yield per hectare)  
• Lower public goods (road density, schools) and literacy (≈ 3 pps lower)  

Direction: negative effect of Zamindari on current economic performance.  
Magnitude: we anticipate −0.15 σ to −0.25 σ in standard-deviation units for composite development index.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (GRDD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Covariate continuity at the cutoff – 0.8  
C2: No manipulation/sorting – 1.0  
C3: Sufficient density of observations near boundary – 0.9  
C4: Functional-form & bandwidth robustness – 0.7  
C5: No confounding policies that jump at border – 0.6  

Overall (average) ≈ 0.8 → design is reasonably credible but will rely on extensive robustness and placebo tests.
